name: Hemp seed oil for hair

card.summary: A plant oil rich in polyunsaturated fats that is used in hair and body care to condition and moisturise hair and scalp.
card.aka: hemp oil, Cannabis sativa seed oil
card.note: Hair-loss claims are supplier or user claims; sources describe cosmetic use rather than regrowth trials.

quick.overview:
Hemp seed oil is pressed from the seeds of low-THC Cannabis sativa varieties. It is mostly polyunsaturated fat, with linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid as the main components, and it appears in shampoos, soaps and body-care products.

Used on hair, it is applied as a conditioning oil with the aim of softer, moisturised hair and a comfortable scalp; some people also take it as a supplement hoping for thicker-looking hair. Hair oils in general are studied mostly for moisture retention and damage reduction.
quick.how: People use it as a pre-wash oil treatment, as an ingredient in shampoos and conditioners, or take it by mouth as a food oil. Results are described as improved softness; claims about reduced shedding come from users and sellers.
quick.risks: Seed oil is cleaned to very low THC levels, with legal limits for THC in foods set in some countries (Canada: 10 ppm, per Wikipedia). Cosmetic oils can cause scalp irritation or allergy in some people.

lead: Hemp seed oil is the edible oil from hempseed, which is about 49% oil by weight. Roughly 76% of the oil is polyunsaturated fat, mainly linoleic acid (about 54%) and alpha-linolenic acid (about 17%).[1] Refined hemp seed oil is used primarily in body care products, soaps and shampoos.[1]

For hair, people use it as a conditioning oil or a supplement. Hair oils work mainly by forming a water-repelling film that reduces moisture loss and limits the swelling and shrinking of the hair shaft when wet, which helps prevent damage; saturated and monounsaturated oils penetrate hair better than polyunsaturated oils.[2] Hemp seed oil is mostly polyunsaturated, so it is typically described as a surface conditioner.[1][2]
Hair oils are marketed for growth, dryness and damage; the evidence available mainly supports moisture retention and damage reduction, while growth claims are less established.[2]

chain: Less moisture loss and surface damage
angle.text: Used as a conditioning oil it can make hair look and feel smoother. Some people also take it hoping for fuller hair.

paras: Refined hemp seed oil is clear and mild-tasting and is used in soaps, shampoos and detergents as well as food.[1]
On hair, it is used as a moisturising or conditioning oil. General hair-oil use dates back to ancient Egypt and India and to Ayurvedic and Unani practice.[2]
The oil contains about 5 to 11% monounsaturated fat and 5 to 7% saturated fat, with an omega-6 to omega-3 ratio of about 3:1.[1]

Hemp seed oil comes from varieties with little THC; seeds are cleaned to 99.99% before pressing, though trace THC can appear from plant matter. Canadian sampling usually finds THC below the 4 ppm detection limit, and Canada's legal food limit is 10 ppm. EU countries differ in their limits.[1]
No studies found. Studies in related areas include a 2005 trial of dietary hempseed oil in atopic dermatitis, cited in the Wikipedia article, which concerns skin rather than hair.[1]
